379.title: The golden calf (Exodus 32)
379.hook: they melt their earrings into a god they can see
379.howItsDone: The Catechism teaches that idolatry includes putting power, pleasure, money or any created thing in God's place, and that venerating holy images is not idolatry, because the honor passes to the person the image represents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Decalogue, which begins with a rescue, not a rule. Your line was freedom first, then the law. Which commandment did you hear as a gift? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

Moses has been up the mountain for forty days. No texts, no updates, just a cloud on the summit and silence. Down in the camp, people start talking. Maybe he's dead. Maybe he's not coming back. And the God he talks to is invisible, up there in the smoke. So they go to Aaron, Moses's brother, the one left in charge, and they say: make us gods to go before us. As for this Moses, we don't know what happened to him. And Aaron says: bring me your gold earrings.
screen: `FORTY DAYS. NO MOSES.` → `MAKE US GODS.` → `BRING ME YOUR EARRINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the calf. Aaron melts the gold and shapes a young bull, and the people say, "These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." Then Aaron builds an altar and announces: tomorrow is a feast of the Lord, using God's own name. That's the twist. They aren't exactly walking away from the God who rescued them. They're trying to make that God visible, portable, controllable. Something they can point at. Second, the excuse. When Moses comes down, sees the dancing and smashes the tablets, he asks his brother what happened. And Aaron says, more or less: they gave me gold, I threw it in the fire, and out came this calf. It's an excuse a parent might hear from a child standing next to a broken vase. Third, the word. An idol, from the Greek eidolon, means an image, even a phantom: something that looks like the real thing and isn't. The Catechism widens it a lot. It says idolatry isn't only about statues: a person commits idolatry whenever they honor a created thing in place of God, and it lists power, pleasure, money, race, the state. Fourth, the obvious question. Catholic churches are full of statues and icons. Are those idols? The Catholic and Orthodox answer comes from a council at Nicaea in 787: the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. In Catholic teaching, the prayer goes to the person, not the plaster. Some Protestant churches, reading the same commandment, keep their walls plain. The real test in Exodus 32 isn't whether there's gold in the room. It's what the people let take God's place.
screen: `THESE ARE THY GODS, O ISRAEL.` · `THIS CALF CAME OUT.` · `EIDOLON: AN IMAGE, A PHANTOM.` · `WHAT TAKES GOD'S PLACE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you put first. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself honestly: what do I check first in the morning? What do I worry about losing most? What would I give up sleep for? Where does my money go when it's tight? Don't judge the answers. Some of them are good things: work, family, health. The calf was made of good gold, too. Just notice which one sits in the center. Then ask if it's where you want it. If you pray, you can set that thing before God and ask for the right order. If you don't, just hold the question for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Idol. From Greek eidolon, an image. Anything, golden or not, that a person lets take the place of God. Today's word.
Your line: what are you worshiping. Today, watch where your attention goes when you're anxious, and ask that question once. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

what it means: a frightened people trying to make God visible and controllable, and letting something take God's place.
what a scholar hears: they name the calf as the God of the Exodus; and the young bull echoes the calves Jeroboam will set up at Bethel and Dan in 1 Kings 12.

380.title: God's back (Exodus 33:18–23)
380.hook: Moses hidden in a cleft of rock sees God pass by
380.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray the examen at night, looking back over the day to notice where God was present, a practice taught by Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and the Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the joy of heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden calf, and today's question about an idol: what takes God's place? Your line was what are you worshiping. What did you find at the center? Day three hundred eighty.

After the calf, after the broken tablets, Moses has one more request, and it's a bold one. He's spoken with God in the cloud. He's heard the voice. Now he wants more. He says four words in the Douay-Rheims: "Shew me thy glory." Not a sign, not a plan, not help with the people. Just: let me see you. A man who has heard the voice many times now asks for the face behind it. And God says yes, and also no.
screen: `AFTER THE CALF, ONE MORE REQUEST.` → `SHEW ME THY GLORY.` → `YES, AND ALSO NO.`

segments.voice: First, the yes. God says: I'll make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll call out my name. Second, the no. "Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me and live." Here's the strange part. Earlier in this same chapter, the text says God spoke to Moses face to face, the way a man speaks to his friend. So which is it? The Bible holds both: real closeness, real conversation, and still a limit. Third, the rock. God says: there's a place by me; stand on the rock. When my glory passes, I'll put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I've gone by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see." The Hebrew word is achorai, my back, what's behind me, after me. Moses sees God only from behind, only as God is going past. Fourth, what Catholic writers made of it. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, said that seeing God's back means following him: you see the back of someone you walk behind. Some readers find a version of this in their own lives: they rarely notice grace in the moment, and see its shape only afterward, looking back at who showed up, which door opened, how they got through. The Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the promise of heaven. Paul says it in a line: we see now through a glass in a dark manner, but then face to face. And centuries later, on another mountain, the Gospels put Moses beside Jesus at the Transfiguration, looking at a face that shines like the sun.
screen: `SHEW ME THY GLORY.` · `NO ONE SEES MY FACE AND LIVES.` · `A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.` · `ACHORAI: SEEN FROM BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back at what carried you. Settle, and breathe. Pick one hard stretch of your life that's over now, or mostly over. Don't relive it. Just walk back through it slowly, like rewinding a video. Who showed up that you didn't expect? What kept you going? What door opened, what phone call came, what small mercy you barely noticed at the time? You're looking at the back of something that already passed by. If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you only see now. If you don't, simply name what carried you. The bell holds the time.
God's back. What Moses saw from a cleft in the rock: God's glory passing by, seen only from behind. Today's word.
Your line: seen from behind. Tonight, look back over the day and find one place where something good passed by that you missed at the time. Day three hundred eighty.

381.title: The dwelling (Exodus 35–40)
381.hook: everyone brings something, and the cloud fills the tent
381.howItsDone: In Catholic churches the Eucharist is reserved in a tabernacle, named after the tent in Exodus, with a lamp kept burning beside it, and parishes rely on volunteers' skills, from musicians and sacristans to cooks and catechists.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God's back: Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing the glory only as it passed. Your line was seen from behind. What good did you notice, looking back? Day three hundred eighty-one.

Here's a sentence you will almost never hear in a parish bulletin: please stop giving, we have too much. It's in Exodus. Moses asks the people to bring materials for a tent where God will dwell among them, and he asks only for what each one's heart moves them to give. And they come, morning after morning, carrying gold jewelry, colored yarn, goat hair, wood, oil, spices. The craftsmen finally go to Moses and say: the people are bringing much more than we need. So Moses sends word through the camp: nobody make anything else for the sanctuary. The people had to be held back from giving.
screen: `FOR WHOEVER'S HEART IS MOVED.` → `MORNING AFTER MORNING.` → `PLEASE STOP. WE HAVE TOO MUCH.`

segments.voice: First, the gifts. The last six chapters of Exodus read like a building inventory, and that's the point: everyone's in it. Rulers bring precious stones. Women who are skilled spin blue and purple and scarlet yarn with their own hands, and some spin goat hair. Others bring their bronze mirrors, and those are melted down for the great washbasin. Nobody's gift is too ordinary. Second, the artist. God calls a craftsman named Bezalel and fills him with the spirit of God, in wisdom and understanding and skill, to work gold, cut stones, carve wood. And what the Spirit gives him, the text says, is skill with his hands. A partner named Oholiab works with him, and they teach others. Third, the dwelling. In Hebrew it's the mishkan, from a verb that means to dwell or to settle. It's a tent, made to be taken down and carried. When it's finished and set up, the cloud covers it, and the glory of the Lord fills it so completely that Moses himself can't go in. The God of the burning mountain now lives in a tent in the middle of the camp. Fourth, where Catholics see it every Sunday. The place in a Catholic church where the Eucharist is kept is called the tabernacle, named for this tent, and for Catholics the lamp burning beside it says what the cloud said: God is here. John's Gospel uses the same picture: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. The Greek verb means, literally, he pitched his tent.
screen: `GOLD, YARN, GOAT HAIR, MIRRORS.` · `BEZALEL, FILLED WITH THE SPIRIT.` · `MISHKAN: THE CLOUD FILLS THE TENT.` · `THE TABERNACLE, NAMED FOR THE TENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one skill you could give. Settle, and breathe. Bezalel's gift was his hands. The women's gift was spinning. Somebody's gift was a mirror. What's yours? Maybe you can cook, fix a sink, keep accounts, sing, drive, sew, read aloud, set up chairs, teach a kid to read. Picture your parish, or any community you belong to, and where that gift would fit. Don't sign up for everything. Just find one place, and picture yourself bringing it. If you pray, you can offer that skill to God. If you don't, simply notice that you have something to bring. The bell holds the time.
The dwelling. The tent built from everyone's gifts, where the cloud of God's glory came to live in the middle of the camp. Today's word.
Your line: everyone brought something. Today, offer one skill to your parish or your community, even an hour, even something small. Day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: Be holy (Leviticus 19)
382.hook: be holy, and thou shalt love thy friend as thyself, and leave gleanings for the poor
382.howItsDone: The Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium teaches the universal call to holiness, and many Catholic parishes run food pantries and collections for the poor; some Catholic groups also organize gleaning on farms after the harvest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dwelling: a tent built from everyone's gifts, filled with the cloud of glory. Your line was everyone brought something. What skill did you offer? Day three hundred eighty-two.

Leviticus has a reputation. It's the book where people who promise to read the whole Bible quietly give up: sacrifices, skin diseases, which animals you can eat. And then, in the middle of it, chapter nineteen opens with a command that sounds enormous. "Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy." You'd expect what follows to be about the temple, or incense, or long prayers. Instead it's about farming. And wages. And how you treat a deaf man and a blind man. Holiness, it turns out, happens in a wheat field.
screen: `THE BOOK PEOPLE GIVE UP ON.` → `BE YE HOLY.` → `HOLINESS IN A WHEAT FIELD.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Holy, in Hebrew kadosh, means set apart, different, belonging to God. The plural, kedoshim, is how the chapter begins, and Jewish tradition still names this section of Leviticus by that word. Second, the corners. When you reap your field, God says, don't harvest all the way to the edges. Don't go back for the stalks you dropped. Don't strip your vineyard bare or pick up the grapes that fell. Leave them for the poor and for the stranger. The edges of your field aren't fully yours. Jewish law still keeps this as peah, the corner, with a whole section of the Mishnah devoted to it. Later in the Bible, a poor foreign widow named Ruth will survive by gathering exactly these leftovers. Third, the list. Pay your worker the same day; don't keep his wages overnight. Don't curse the deaf, and don't put a stumbling block in front of the blind. Stand up for the old. Use honest weights in the market. Love the stranger as yourself, because you were strangers in Egypt. And in the middle of it all, the line Jesus will later call the second great commandment. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says it this way: "Thou shalt love thy friend as thyself." Most English Bibles say neighbor. The Hebrew word, rea, can mean either. Fourth, what the Church draws from it. The Second Vatican Council taught that every baptized person, not only priests and nuns, is called to holiness. Leviticus nineteen shows what that looks like at ground level: in the paycheck, the market, the harvest, and what you leave at the edges for someone else.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `LEAVE THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.` · `HONEST WAGES, HONEST WEIGHTS.` · `LOVE THY FRIEND AS THYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something for someone else. Settle, and breathe. Think about your own fields: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your parking spot, the last slice of something. Where are the corners you usually harvest right to the edge? Pick one, and plan to leave it. A bag of groceries for the food pantry. A generous tip. Ten minutes that go to someone else instead of your inbox. The last good seat. If you pray, you can offer that corner to God. If you don't, simply choose it, and picture who might find it. The bell holds the time.
Be holy. The command that opens Leviticus nineteen, lived out in fields, wages, and the corners left for the poor. Today's word.
Your line: leave the corners. Today, don't take everything you could; leave one corner of your time, money or food for someone else. Day three hundred eighty-two.

383.title: Jubilee (Leviticus 25)
383.hook: every fiftieth year debts forgiven and land returned; the Church still keeps holy years
383.howItsDone: The Catholic Church proclaims ordinary jubilee years, when pilgrims pass through the holy doors of Rome's major basilicas and seek reconciliation, and popes have also called extraordinary jubilees, such as the Year of Mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, be holy: holiness in wheat fields and paychecks. Your line was leave the corners. What corner did you leave for someone else? Day three hundred eighty-three.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell, the Liberty Bell, with a line of scripture running around its top about proclaiming liberty throughout all the land to all its inhabitants. It's from Leviticus, chapter twenty-five. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, words it differently: "proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land." Liberty or remission, the verse wasn't first about a nation's independence. It was about a year. A strange, radical year that came around once every half century.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `PROCLAIM LIBERTY.` → `ONCE EVERY HALF CENTURY.`

segments.voice: First, the count. Every seventh year in Israel was a sabbath for the land: no planting, the fields rest. Count seven of those, forty-nine years, and the next one, the fiftieth, is the jubilee. It begins on the Day of Atonement with a blast on the ram's horn through the whole land. The year's Hebrew name, yovel, is traditionally linked to that ram's horn, and it's where the word jubilee comes from. Second, what happens. Land that a family sold in hard times goes back to them. People who sold themselves into service because of debt go free and return to their families. The land rests again. And God gives the reason: the land is mine, and you are strangers and guests with me. Nobody gets to own it forever. Third, the honest question. Did Israel ever fully keep it? The sources are mostly silent, and scholars still debate it. But the idea never went away. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, he read from Isaiah about the acceptable year of the Lord, and some readers hear in it the language of jubilee. Fourth, the Catholic holy year. In 1300, Pope Boniface the Eighth proclaimed the first Christian jubilee, a year of pilgrimage and forgiveness in Rome. The Church still keeps them. In Rome, special holy doors are opened that stay sealed between jubilees. And before the year 2000, Pope John Paul the Second called for the debts of the poorest nations to be reduced or forgiven, a jubilee for whole countries. Some word historians think the Latin heard yovel alongside iubilare, to shout for joy, which may be why our word sounds like joy.
screen: `SEVEN SEVENS, THEN THE FIFTIETH.` · `YOVEL: THE RAM'S HORN SOUNDS.` · `LAND RETURNS, DEBTORS GO FREE.` · `HOLY YEARS AND HOLY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one debt, big or small. Settle, and breathe. Think about what people owe you. Maybe money: twenty dollars a friend never paid back. Maybe something else: an apology you're still waiting for, a favor you keep score of, a sibling who never pulled their weight. Pick one. Picture writing it off, the way the horn would sound and the slate would clear. You don't have to tell them. You just stop collecting. If you pray, you can say the line from the Our Father as Matthew gives it: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." If you don't, picture the ledger closing. The bell holds the time.
Jubilee. From yovel, the ram's horn: the fiftieth year, when land returned and debtors went free. The Church still keeps holy years. Today's word.
Your line: a year to set free. Today, let one person off the hook for something they owe you, and don't keep the receipt. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: The blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
384.hook: the Lord bless thee and keep thee: the priestly blessing still used at Mass
384.howItsDone: The priestly blessing from Numbers 6 is read at Mass on January 1, the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, and some solemn blessings at the end of Mass use its words; some Catholic parents also trace a cross on their children's foreheads with a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jubilee: the ram's horn, the fiftieth year, land returned and debts set free. Your line was a year to set free. Whose debt did you let go? Day three hundred eighty-four.

Near the end of a Mass, the people stop speaking, and something is said over them. A hand goes up, and the room hears words it didn't earn and didn't ask for. In the book of Numbers, God gives Moses three short lines for exactly this. They aren't a prayer for the people to memorize and recite. They're a blessing, meant to be spoken over someone else, by someone else. And on some Sundays, those three lines from the desert are still spoken over a Catholic congregation before it goes home.
screen: `NEAR THE END OF MASS.` → `SAID OVER, NOT SAID BY.` → `THREE LINES FROM THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: First, who gives it. In the book of Numbers, God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people. Then the words, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee. The Lord shew his face to thee, and have mercy on thee. The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace." Second, its shape. In Hebrew, the first line has three words, the second five, the third seven. It grows as it goes, like a wave building. And it moves from keeping you safe, to looking at you with mercy, to peace, shalom, a word that reaches past quiet toward wholeness. Third, the face. Two of the three lines are about God's face. To have someone's face shine on you, or turn toward you, is the picture of being seen with delight. A child looking for a parent in the crowd at a school play knows exactly what that means. And at the end, God says: so they shall put my name on the people, and I will bless them. The priests speak; God does the blessing. Fourth, where Catholics hear it. On the first of January, the feast of Mary, Mother of God, it's the first reading at Mass. One of the solemn blessings a priest may give at the end of Mass in Ordinary Time uses its words. Saint Francis of Assisi wrote it out by hand for his friend Brother Leo, and that scrap of parchment still survives in Assisi. Jewish priests' descendants still give this blessing in synagogue, hands raised over the people.
screen: `THIS IS HOW YOU SHALL BLESS.` · `THREE WORDS, FIVE, THEN SEVEN.` · `HIS FACE, MERCY, AND PEACE.` · `AT MASS, AND IN FRANCIS'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone with these words. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind. Someone you love, someone who's struggling, maybe someone you find hard. Picture their face. Then, if you're comfortable, say the blessing for them, slowly, silently or aloud: the Lord bless thee, and keep thee. Pause. The Lord show his face to thee, and have mercy on thee. Pause. The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace. If you don't pray, you can simply wish them those three things: safety, being seen with kindness, and peace. Stay with their face a little while. The bell holds the time.
The blessing. The priestly blessing of Numbers six: keeping, a shining face, mercy and peace. Still heard at Mass. Today's word.
Your line: the lord bless thee. Today, bless one person, out loud or in your heart, with these words or with a simple may you have peace. Day three hundred eighty-four.

385.title: The spies (Numbers 13–14)
385.hook: ten saw giants, two saw a land of milk and honey
385.howItsDone: The Catholic Church counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given in confirmation, and the Catechism describes it as firmness in difficulty that enables a person to conquer fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing: keeping, a shining face, mercy and peace. Your line was the lord bless thee. Who did you bless? Today closes a week that ran from the golden calf through God's back, the dwelling, be holy and the jubilee. Day three hundred eighty-five.

Twelve men come back from a forty-day scouting trip, and two of them are carrying a single cluster of grapes on a pole between them. That's how big the grapes are. They also bring pomegranates and figs. The whole camp crowds around. And the report starts well: it's a land flowing with milk and honey, just as promised. Here's the fruit. And then the word but. But the people there are strong. The cities are great and walled. And we saw giants. Next to them we were like grasshoppers, and that's how we looked to them.
screen: `TWELVE SCOUTS, FORTY DAYS.` → `GRAPES CARRIED ON A POLE.` → `BUT WE SAW GIANTS.`

segments.voice: First, two reports from one trip. All twelve saw the same land: the same fruit, the same walls, the same tall people. Ten came back saying we can't. Two, Caleb and Joshua, came back saying we can. Caleb quiets the crowd and says, let's go up at once and take it, for we are well able. In Hebrew he doubles the verb, which is a way of insisting: we can, we surely can. Second, the grasshopper line. Read it again. We were grasshoppers in our own sight, and so we were in theirs. How would they know what the giants thought? They never asked. They decided how small they were, and then assumed everyone else agreed. Third, the night of weeping. The whole people cry all night. Let's choose a leader and go back to Egypt, they say. Back to the bricks. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: the land is very good; don't be afraid; the Lord is with us. And the crowd talks about stoning them. Fourth, the cost. A whole generation decides it can't, and the text takes them at their word. Forty years in the wilderness, a year for each day of scouting, until that generation has passed, and only Caleb and Joshua, of all those twenty and older who were counted, will walk into the land. The Church names this courage fortitude, one of the four cardinal virtues. The Catechism says it gives firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good, and that it enables a person to conquer fear. Not to feel no fear. To conquer it.
screen: `SAME LAND, TWO REPORTS.` · `GRASSHOPPERS IN OUR OWN SIGHT.` · `A NIGHT OF WEEPING FOR EGYPT.` · `FORTITUDE: TO CONQUER FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one fear differently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that feels like a giant right now. A deadline, a conversation, a health worry, a new job. Notice the story you're telling about it, and about yourself next to it. Am I deciding I'm a grasshopper before anyone else has? Then look at the same situation the way Caleb did. Same walls, same giants. But what's the fruit? What's good on the other side? Hold both. If you pray, you can bring that fear to God and listen for Caleb's words. If you don't, just try on the second report for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The spies. Twelve scouts who saw the same land: ten saw giants and fear, two saw milk and honey and said we can. Today's word.
Your line: we are able. Today, when you catch yourself shrinking to grasshopper size, ask who told you that, and give the second report. Day three hundred eighty-five.

fork.setup: you're Caleb. ten of your fellow scouts have just told the crowd about walls and giants, and the people are getting loud. what do you say?
options: they're right. let's find another way.
quiet the people: let's go up at once, for we are well able.
say nothing and let Moses handle it.
fork.reveal: he quiets the crowd and says let's go up and take it, we are well able. the crowd doesn't listen, and that night they weep for Egypt.

original.note: Hebrew: we are surely able. Caleb doubles the verb to insist (Numbers 13:30).

trapdoor: what you thought: a war story about giants.
what it means: twelve men saw the same land, and ten let fear tell them how small they were.
what a scholar hears: Caleb's doubled verb, yakhol nukhal, insists we can; and the forty years match the forty days, a year for each day.
